title: The Wishing Ring

evidence.note: Released November 9, 1914 in the US by World Film Manufacturing Company (distributed as 'A Shubert Feature'). The US copyright term for works published in 1914 has expired, so the film print is public domain in the US by term expiry.
evidence.source: Silent Era Progressive Silent Film List

evidence.note: The film is silent, so the images carry no soundtrack of their own. Any music on a modern copy is a separate recording or composition and may be protected by its own copyright or licence.

The film is based on Owen Davis's play 'The Wishing Ring' (per Silent Era). I could not confirm the play's publication date or its registration and renewal history, so the story layer is not marked as cleared.
evidence.source: Silent Era Progressive Silent Film List

evidence.note: Silent Era says a print exists at the Library of Congress and that a 35mm restoration was made from a British reduction print. I could not identify who made that restoration or whether it added a new score or titles. If it did, those additions could be protected.

editorial:
The Wishing Ring: An Idyll of Old England is a silent comedy-drama released November 9, 1914 by World Film Manufacturing Company as a Shubert Feature. Maurice Tourneur directed it. Vivian Martin plays Sally, the parson's daughter, Alec B. Francis the Earl of Bateson and Chester Barnett his son Giles. A creator gets an early Tourneur feature that survives, with a print held at the Library of Congress.

The film print is public domain in the US because the copyright term for 1914 publications has expired. Other layers are not cleared. The film adapts Owen Davis's play, and I could not confirm that play's publication or registration history, so check it before relying on the story. Any music on a modern copy is a separate work, and a restored copy may carry added material. Use the images with your own score or one you have cleared.
faq: Can I reuse the 1914 film footage of The Wishing Ring in the US?
The film print is public domain in the US because the copyright term for 1914 publications has expired. Check separately for any added score, titles or other new material in the copy you use.
Is the story free to adapt too?
Not confirmed. The film is based on Owen Davis's play, and I could not verify that play's publication or registration history. Check it before making a new adaptation of the story itself.
